title: How Many Hotels Actually Use AI, and Is Yours Ready?
summary: Two 2026 surveys put hotel AI adoption at 98%. Original research across 26,707 hotels in Germany, Austria and Switzerland shows only about one in ten has any guest-facing automation. Here is why both numbers are true.
body_markdown:
Common questions


## FAQ


### How many hotels use AI in 2026?


By self-report, almost all of them: two independent 2026 surveys, from Mews and from Wyndham, both put hotel AI adoption at 98%. But adoption and integration are different measures. Wyndham found only 32% of owners say AI is embedded across most of their operations, and BCG's 2026 work with NYU found fewer than 10% of hospitality companies are "future built" with AI generating substantial value.


In our own enrichment of 26,707 hotels in Germany, Austria and Switzerland with live websites, only about 10% show any guest-facing automation at all, and 0.37% reach the top rung. Most hotels have started with AI; far fewer have wired it into how they run.


### What does AI adoption actually look like in hotels?


Mostly chat-first and text-first: a website chat widget, a messaging autoresponder, or a bot that answers common questions in text. That is the ordinary case and it is genuine. Voice, meaning an AI that answers the phone and acts on the request, is earlier and less common. Voice connected to the property management system, able to complete a booking end to end, is rarer still.


The industry's 98% adoption figure counts the chat widget and the end-to-end system as the same thing, which is why the headline number and the reality on the ground look so different.


### Are hotels in Germany and Austria using AI for phone calls?


Mostly not yet. In our DACH data, 27.9% of hotels have no 24/7 reception, and for a large share of the market the phone is still the primary booking channel by design rather than a legacy one.


AI voice on the hotel line is one of the earliest and least-adopted layers, even though it is where a lot of the demand and the missed revenue actually sits. The precondition is a line that gets answered reliably and a system the AI can read and write.


### Why is there such a gap between AI adoption surveys and reality?


Because a survey measures whether a hotel has used AI at all, and a hotel that added a chatbot in 2024 answers yes. Operational integration, AI wired across bookings, the phone, and the property management system, is a different and much smaller thing.


The measured integration figures are small everywhere: 32% "embedded across most operations" in Wyndham's survey, fewer than 10% "future built" in BCG's, and 0.37% at the top rung of guest-facing automation in our DACH data. The gap is not a contradiction; it is the difference between starting and finishing.


### What has to be in place before a hotel can use an AI phone agent?


Two things above all: a phone line that is actually answered, or that has a clear coverage gap an agent can fill, and a property management system the agent can read and write so it can complete a request rather than just take a message. A working direct-booking engine helps, since it gives the AI somewhere to send a completed booking.


The pattern across the market is that the base arrives before the intelligence, so the useful first question is not "which AI" but "is the infrastructure underneath it real yet."
